title: Chapter 9 Drill: Headache, Pain, Sleep, and Autonomic Disorders

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with heart failure has recurrent cycles of waxing and waning breathing with apneas without respiratory effort during sleep. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Obstructive sleep apnea with upper airway collapse
Central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing
items.explanation: Crescendo-decrescendo breathing with apneas that lack respiratory effort characterizes Cheyne-Stokes central sleep apnea, common in heart failure and after stroke. Obstructive apnea shows persistent effort against a closed airway. Obesity hypoventilation involves sustained hypercapnia, and resistance syndrome causes arousals without frank apneas. Treating the heart failure is the first step. Because the underlying pathophysiology differs from obstruction, therapy targets the cause, with adaptive servo ventilation avoided when ejection fraction is low.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has posterior neck pain radiating to the occiput, reproduced by neck movement and relieved temporarily by a greater occipital nerve block. Imaging shows cervical spondylosis. What is the likely headache type?
items.explanation: Cervicogenic headache arises from cervical structures, is provoked by neck movement or pressure, and follows a diagnostic block of the implicated nerve or joint. Cluster headache and hemicrania continua show prominent autonomic features, and primary stabbing headache consists of seconds-long jabs. Occipital nerve blocks serve as both diagnostic and therapeutic tools, and physical therapy and posture correction support long-term control.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has continuous right-sided headache for 4 months with superimposed severe attacks, ipsilateral conjunctival injection, and tearing. She has had no response to triptans. Which drug is expected to produce complete resolution?
items.explanation: Hemicrania continua is a strictly unilateral continuous headache with autonomic features that responds absolutely to indomethacin, which is also diagnostic. Paroxysmal hemicrania shares this response. Triptans do not control it. Carbamazepine is used for trigeminal neuralgia, and naproxen is not reliably effective in the indomethacin-responsive headaches. A therapeutic trial with a full dose for a week or two is both diagnostic and curative, and imaging should still exclude a structural cause.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl wakes 2 hours after sleep onset screaming, with a racing heart, and cannot be consoled for 5 minutes before returning to sleep. She recalls nothing. What is the best management?
options: Brain MRI and prolonged video EEG at once
Reassurance, safe sleep environment, and consistent sleep schedule
items.explanation: Sleep terrors are a benign non-REM arousal disorder of early childhood, often improved by adequate sleep and a safe environment, and parents should not wake the child. Medication and extensive testing are unwarranted for typical events. Polysomnography is considered only for atypical, injurious, or frequent episodes that suggest seizures or apnea. A scheduled awakening before the usual event time can help when events are frequent, and parents should remove hazards and lock windows and doors.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man has brief, stabbing ice-pick pains in the temple lasting 2 seconds, occurring several times daily without autonomic features. Examination is normal. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Urgent cerebral angiography and neurosurgical review
Carbamazepine at the maximum tolerated dose
High-flow oxygen at 12 liters per minute
items.explanation: Primary stabbing headache causes transient jabs lasting seconds with no other features, and responds to indomethacin when treatment is wanted. Imaging is needed only with atypical features. Oxygen is for cluster headache, and carbamazepine is not a typical choice. Indomethacin is used for only the minority needing treatment, with gastric protection, because most patients are reassured by the benign nature of the pain.

items.stem: A 58-year-old obese man has loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headaches, and hypertension. A home sleep apnea test shows an apnea hypopnea index of 32 per hour. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Oral appliance for tongue stimulation only
items.explanation: Moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea is treated first with CPAP, which reduces sleepiness, blood pressure, and cardiovascular risk, alongside weight loss. Modafinil treats residual sleepiness but not the airway collapse. Sedative hypnotics can worsen apnea. Oral appliances suit mild disease or CPAP intolerance rather than severe disease as first choice. Adherence should be checked with device downloads, and weight loss, positional therapy, and treatment of nasal obstruction support but rarely replace pressure therapy.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy sleeps from 4 a.m. to 1 p.m. on weekends and 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. on school days, with severe morning sleepiness at school. Actigraphy shows sleep extension on free days. What is the most likely contributor?
options: Insufficient sleep and delayed circadian phase
Idiopathic hypersomnia with long sleep time
items.explanation: A large gap between school-day and weekend sleep with catch-up sleep shows chronic sleep restriction, often combined with the delayed circadian phase of adolescence. Treatment includes earlier consistent wake time, morning light, and reduced evening screens. Narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia require sleepiness despite adequate sleep, and apnea needs respiratory events. Sleep extension on free days is the clue, so a trial of regular adequate sleep resolves the symptoms and avoids unnecessary stimulant treatment.

items.stem: A 19-year-old college student has daily irresistible sleep episodes, sudden bilateral knee buckling when laughing, vivid hallucinations at sleep onset, and awakening paralysis. Which finding is most likely on cerebrospinal fluid testing?
options: Elevated oligoclonal bands with a raised IgG index on cerebrospinal fluid
Markedly elevated protein with normal cells
Hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) level at or below 110 pg/mL
items.explanation: Cataplexy with excessive sleepiness defines narcolepsy type 1, associated with loss of hypocretin neurons and CSF hypocretin-1 at or below 110 pg/mL. Oligoclonal bands indicate intrathecal inflammation as in multiple sclerosis. The 14-3-3 protein suggests prion disease, and very high protein with few cells reflects albuminocytologic dissociation seen in Guillain-Barre syndrome. The cerebrospinal fluid test is reserved for cases where sleep testing is unclear, such as patients on interfering drugs or with an uncertain latency study.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has attacks of severe right orbital pain lasting 45 minutes, up to three times a day for 5 weeks, with ipsilateral tearing, nasal congestion, and ptosis. He paces the room during attacks. Which treatment aborts an individual attack most reliably?
options: Oral ibuprofen at a high dose taken at the first sign of every single attack
High-flow oxygen at 12 to 15 liters per minute by non-rebreather mask
items.explanation: Cluster headache is aborted with 100 percent oxygen at 12 to 15 liters per minute for about 15 minutes or with subcutaneous sumatriptan or intranasal zolmitriptan. Oral tablets act too slowly for a peak pain that arrives within minutes. Nonsteroidal drugs have little effect, and magnesium has no role in aborting a cluster attack. Treat early, since oxygen works best within minutes of onset, and confirm the patient can access a regulator and non-rebreather mask at home.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has brief electric shocks in the right cheek triggered by chewing and a light breeze, lasting seconds, with no sensory loss. Which drug is the best initial treatment?
items.explanation: Classical trigeminal neuralgia causes paroxysmal lancinating pain in a trigeminal division with triggers and no deficit, usually from neurovascular compression. Carbamazepine, or oxcarbazepine, is first line. Gabapentin and tricyclics are weaker options, and steroids are not helpful. Monitor sodium, and consider microvascular decompression if drugs fail. Baseline sodium, liver tests, and HLA-B*1502 testing in at-risk ancestry groups reduce serious adverse effects, and the dose is titrated slowly.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, constipation, and urinary retention. He has no parkinsonism, cerebellar signs, or cognitive impairment. Plasma norepinephrine is low when supine and does not rise on standing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Pure autonomic failure is an isolated postganglionic synucleinopathy, with low supine norepinephrine that fails to rise on standing, indicating peripheral noradrenergic denervation. In multiple system atrophy the lesion is preganglionic, so supine norepinephrine is normal. Diabetic neuropathy needs diabetes, and Parkinson disease would show motor features. Distinguishing preganglionic from postganglionic failure changes prognosis, so catecholamine testing and a careful search for parkinsonism, ataxia, and stridor are worthwhile.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has chronic migraine with 20 headache days a month and has failed topiramate and propranolol. Which preventive therapy has randomized evidence in chronic migraine and targets the neuropeptide pathway?
options: Daily acetazolamide titrated to the maximum tolerated dose
A monoclonal antibody against the CGRP ligand or its receptor
Long-term daily oral ergotamine for prevention
Oral prednisone monthly for each cycle
items.explanation: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and eptinezumab reduce monthly migraine days and are approved for prevention, including chronic migraine. Onabotulinumtoxin A is another evidence-based option for chronic migraine. Acetazolamide, ergotamine, and steroids lack this support, and chronic ergotamine risks ergotism and overuse headache. Injection or infusion frequency varies, constipation and injection reactions can occur, and long-term safety data are accumulating as more patients are treated.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman fractured her wrist 6 weeks ago. Her hand is now swollen, warm, and extremely painful with allodynia, color change, and stiffness out of proportion to the injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cellulitis of the hand with early abscess
Carpal tunnel syndrome with thenar wasting
items.explanation: Disproportionate pain with autonomic, sensory, motor, and trophic changes after limb injury without a nerve lesion defines complex regional pain syndrome type 1, diagnosed by the Budapest criteria. Management stresses early physical and occupational therapy, with neuropathic agents and bisphosphonates in selected cases. Infection and entrapment lack this pattern. Early rehabilitation improves outcome, and sympathetic blocks or spinal cord stimulation are considered if progressive symptoms persist despite conservative measures.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has headache after a mild concussion 5 weeks ago, with dizziness and poor concentration. Neurologic examination and head CT are normal. What is the best approach?
options: Education and reassurance, graded activity, and treatment of the headache phenotype
Bed rest in a dark room for several weeks
items.explanation: Persistent post-traumatic headache is common after mild head injury and often resembles migraine or tension-type headache, which guides treatment. Early return to graded activity improves recovery, while prolonged rest delays it. Opioids invite overuse headache, and puncture is unnecessary without red flags. Reassessment at several weeks identifies those with persistent symptoms who benefit from rehabilitation, vestibular therapy, or cognitive support.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man with a T4 complete spinal cord injury develops pounding headache, flushing above the level of injury, and blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg. What is the first step in management?
options: Obtain urgent head CT before any intervention
Give sublingual nifedipine only and observe
Sit him upright and loosen tight clothing, then check the bladder and bowel
items.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia follows a noxious stimulus below an injury at or above T6, most often a distended bladder or fecal impaction. Immediate care is upright positioning, removal of constricting items, and finding and relieving the trigger, with antihypertensives if pressure stays elevated. Naloxone has no role, and head CT delays removal of the cause. Recurring episodes require a bladder program and bowel regimen, and some patients carry nifedipine or nitrate for emergencies while help is arranged.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with narcolepsy type 1 has persistent daytime sleepiness and cataplexy. She is started on sodium oxybate. Which counseling point is essential?
options: Take with a high-fat meal at bedtime only and avoid any second dose in the night
Combine with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Do not combine with sedatives, and expect a second dose in the night
Use it freely with other central depressants
items.explanation: Sodium oxybate improves cataplexy and sleepiness but depresses the central nervous system, and has a boxed warning for respiratory depression and misuse. It is dosed at bedtime and again 2.5 to 4 hours later, on an empty stomach since food reduces absorption. Combination with sedatives is contraindicated. Women of childbearing age should be counseled about contraception, and patients should not drive or operate machinery for several hours after dosing.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy snores nightly with mouth breathing, restless sleep, and daytime inattention. Examination shows enlarged tonsils. What is the best first treatment?
options: Continuous positive airway pressure as the first choice
items.explanation: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the leading cause of obstructive sleep apnea in children, and adenotonsillectomy is first-line when tonsils are enlarged. CPAP is for those who are not candidates or have residual disease. Stimulants would treat a symptom rather than the cause, and melatonin does not relieve airway obstruction. Polysomnography first confirms the diagnosis, and persistent disease after surgery, obesity, or craniofacial abnormalities may require further evaluation and positive pressure.

items.stem: During polysomnography, which electroencephalographic finding defines stage N2 sleep?
options: Sawtooth waves with rapid eye movements
Delta waves in over 20 percent of the epoch
Alpha rhythm that attenuates with eye opening
items.explanation: Stage N2 is marked by 12 to 14 Hz sleep spindles and K complexes on a low-voltage background. Sawtooth waves accompany REM sleep, and slow delta activity of more than 20 percent of an epoch defines N3. Posterior alpha rhythm with eye closure marks relaxed wakefulness, and its loss with drowsiness introduces stage N1. Counting these features, together with rapid eye movements and muscle tone changes, lets the scorer assign each thirty second epoch to the correct stage.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man had herpes zoster of the left thoracic dermatome 4 months ago. Burning pain and allodynia persist in that area. Which topical agent is appropriate when oral drugs are not tolerated?
items.explanation: Postherpetic neuralgia is treated with gabapentinoids, tricyclics, or serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, with topical lidocaine patches or high-concentration capsaicin as local options. Steroid creams and anti-inflammatory gels do not act on neuropathic pain, and compresses provide no meaningful relief. Early antiviral treatment and vaccination reduce its occurrence. Capsaicin at high concentration applied under supervision is another option, and early antiviral therapy with zoster vaccination lowers the risk of this complication.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has diffuse musculoskeletal pain, nonrestorative sleep, fatigue, and cognitive complaints for 2 years. Examination and routine laboratory tests are normal. Which intervention has the strongest evidence?
options: Aerobic exercise with cognitive behavioral therapy and, if needed, duloxetine or pregabalin
items.explanation: Fibromyalgia is managed with education, graded aerobic exercise, sleep care, and cognitive behavioral therapy, with duloxetine, milnacipran, or pregabalin for selected patients. Opioids and steroids lack benefit and add harm, and inactivity worsens pain and fatigue. Patient education and realistic goals are central, since the condition is chronic and fluctuating but not progressive or damaging to joints.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness for 3 weeks. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 98 mm per hour. What should be done immediately?
options: Wait for temporal artery biopsy results before starting any glucocorticoid therapy
Prescribe a triptan for presumed migraine
Start high-dose glucocorticoids before biopsy results
items.explanation: Giant cell arteritis threatens vision from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, which is often irreversible. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily, begin at once when suspicion is high, because biopsy remains informative for at least a couple of weeks of therapy. Delay risks blindness, and aspirin or a triptan does not suppress the arteritis.

items.stem: A 29-year-old obese woman has daily headaches, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus. Examination shows bilateral papilledema with normal cranial nerves, and MRI and MR venography are normal. Opening pressure is 36 cm of water with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. Which is the first-line medical therapy?
options: Repeated daily lumbar punctures as sole therapy
items.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is treated with weight reduction and acetazolamide, which reduces cerebrospinal fluid production, aimed at preserving vision. Topiramate is an alternative. Steroids are not advised, and repeated punctures are only a temporizing step. Progressive visual loss despite therapy prompts optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting. Serial visual fields and formal perimetry guide response, and pregnancy or cognitive concerns should be addressed before choosing an alternative drug.

items.stem: A 8-year-old girl has recurrent bilateral frontal headaches, nausea, and photophobia lasting 2 hours, with normal examination. What is the best acute therapy?
options: Sumatriptan injection at a pediatric dose
Daily topiramate taken for each attack
items.explanation: Pediatric migraine is shorter and often bilateral, and first-line acute treatment is ibuprofen or acetaminophen at weight-based doses, with certain triptans approved for adolescents. Ergotamine is not recommended, and topiramate is a preventive, not an acute drug. Adequate fluids, sleep, and regular meals are important nonpharmacologic measures, and a headache diary identifies triggers that can be avoided.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea cannot tolerate CPAP and has a body mass index of 33. Which alternative is approved for selected patients with an apnea hypopnea index under 50?
options: Nightly modafinil at a standard dose
items.explanation: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation advances the tongue during inspiration and is approved for selected patients with moderate to severe disease and body mass index below 35 after CPAP failure. Modafinil treats sleepiness only, benzodiazepines worsen apnea, and oxygen alone does not prevent obstruction. Drug-induced sleep endoscopy helps select candidates, and weight loss, positional therapy, and mandibular advancement remain options for other patients.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman flies from New York to Paris for a week. On arrival she has early-evening sleepiness and awakens at 3 a.m. Which strategy best speeds adaptation after eastward travel?
options: Seek bright light in the evening and take melatonin at local wake time
Seek bright morning light and take melatonin at local bedtime
Avoid all light for the first week
Take a stimulant at local bedtime
items.explanation: Eastward travel requires advancing the circadian clock, using morning light after the body-clock minimum and melatonin at the new bedtime. Evening light delays the clock, which helps westward travel instead. Light avoidance and bedtime stimulants do not realign the rhythm and can aggravate insomnia. Sunglasses can limit evening light on arrival, and remaining awake until local evening, with a short nap only early in the day, speeds adjustment.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man reports lightheadedness on standing. Supine blood pressure is 148/84 mm Hg with heart rate 70. After 3 minutes standing, it is 112/68 with heart rate 72. What does the heart rate response suggest?
options: Hypovolemia from acute gastrointestinal blood loss
Postural tachycardia syndrome with hyperadrenergic features
items.explanation: A fall of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic mm Hg with minimal heart rate rise (under 15 beats per minute, or a ratio of heart rate change to systolic fall below 0.5) indicates failure of the baroreflex efferent arc, meaning neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Hypovolemia typically produces a brisk tachycardia. POTS requires a rise of 30 beats without hypotension.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman takes combination analgesics on 18 days each month for chronic migraine. Her headache is now present most days and responds poorly to treatment. What is the best first step in management?
options: Increase the dose of the combination analgesic to gain control of each daily headache before any other step
Order MRI of the brain with gadolinium before any change
Educate and withdraw the overused analgesic while starting a preventive medication
Switch her to a daily long-acting opioid
items.explanation: Medication overuse headache occurs when simple analgesics are used 15 or more days a month, or triptans, opioids, and combination products 10 or more days a month. Management combines education, withdrawal of the culprit, and preventive therapy started early. More analgesic perpetuates the cycle, imaging adds little without red flags, and opioids worsen chronicity and are not advised.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man has bilateral pressing headaches without nausea, lasting several hours, about twice a week, relieved by ibuprofen. He is otherwise well. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate headache without nausea or marked photophobia, unaggravated by routine activity, defines tension-type headache. Simple analgesics treat acute episodes. Migraine would be throbbing, worsened by movement, and include nausea. Hemicrania continua is strictly unilateral, and cervicogenic headache arises from the neck with restricted movement. Chronic forms are defined by headache on at least fifteen days monthly for three months, and psychological stress and muscle tenderness frequently contribute.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with cluster headache is entering a bout. He needs a transitional therapy while a long-term preventive reaches effect. Which agent is the best choice for the long-term preventive?
options: Amitriptyline at bedtime, with a baseline electrocardiogram and slow dose escalation
Verapamil, with an electrocardiogram before dose escalation
items.explanation: Verapamil is first-line prevention for cluster headache, often at doses of 240 mg a day or more, and requires ECG monitoring for PR prolongation and heart block as the dose rises. A short course of prednisone or an occipital nerve block can bridge. Amitriptyline and topiramate have weak support, and as-needed propranolol cannot prevent attacks.

items.stem: A 35-year-old nurse working rotating night shifts has severe sleepiness during night work and poor daytime sleep for 6 months. Which intervention best reduces her sleepiness during shifts?
options: Permanent abrupt return to a day schedule
Scheduled bright light during the shift and light avoidance on the commute home
items.explanation: Shift work disorder responds to timed bright light early in the night shift, dark sunglasses on the way home, and a regular daytime sleep window in a dark room, with melatonin before daytime sleep and modafinil or armodafinil for shift alertness. Light after work delays adaptation, and hypnotics alone do not shift the circadian phase. Caffeine in the first half of the shift and strategic naps add benefit, while avoiding heavy meals and bright light before daytime sleep.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has headaches for 8 days a month and is considering a preventive. She has depression and obesity. Which agent addresses both conditions and migraine?
options: Amitriptyline or venlafaxine, with weight and mood monitoring
items.explanation: Antidepressants such as amitriptyline and venlafaxine prevent migraine and treat depression, though amitriptyline causes weight gain, so choice requires balance. Beta-blockers can worsen depression, and valproate promotes weight gain and is teratogenic. Titration should be gradual, and any side effects such as sedation, weight gain, or blood pressure elevation should guide the final choice of agent.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has palpitations, fatigue, and lightheadedness on standing for 8 months. Heart rate rises from 74 to 118 within 10 minutes of standing, with blood pressure stable. Which is the best first-line nonpharmacologic measure?
options: Increased fluid and salt intake with graded exercise
Compression stockings alone and no exercise
items.explanation: POTS is defined by a sustained heart rate rise of 30 beats per minute or more (40 in teenagers) within 10 minutes without orthostatic hypotension, with symptoms over 3 months. Volume expansion with fluids and salt, and gradual recumbent then upright exercise reconditioning, are the foundation. Bed rest worsens deconditioning, and sympathomimetic drugs would aggravate tachycardia. Abdominal binders, compression garments, and avoiding prolonged standing in heat can be added when symptoms persist despite these first measures.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with migraine has severe attacks that cluster around her menses. She wants to conceive within a year. Which acute treatment is generally considered safest?
options: Ergotamine tartrate taken together with caffeine
items.explanation: Acetaminophen is first choice in pregnancy, and sumatriptan has reassuring registry data when needed. Ergotamine is contraindicated because of uterine vasoconstriction. Valproate carries a major teratogenic risk and is avoided in women of childbearing potential, and topiramate is linked to oral clefts and low birth weight. Folic acid supplementation before conception, and a plan to transition preventive drugs well ahead of pregnancy, completes the counseling for this patient.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with narcolepsy type 1 is given modafinil for sleepiness. Which counseling point is most important regarding her contraception?
options: Modafinil raises estrogen levels and clot risk
No interaction exists with hormonal agents
Modafinil can reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives
items.explanation: Modafinil and armodafinil induce CYP3A4 and can lower hormonal contraceptive levels, so a backup or alternative method is advised and counseling about pregnancy planning is needed. They also can cause headache, anxiety, and rare severe rash. The claim of raised estrogen and clots is incorrect, and no drug of this class offers contraception. Pregnancy planning is another reason to review her regimen, because safety data are limited and the lowest dose should be used if therapy continues.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man shouts and punches during sleep, once injuring his wife. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia. What is the most important implication of this diagnosis?
options: High risk of later alpha-synucleinopathy such as Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia
High risk of later multiple sclerosis
High risk of later amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
High risk of later primary angiitis of the central nervous system
items.explanation: Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder is a strong prodrome of synucleinopathy, with most patients converting to Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or multiple system atrophy over years. The other disorders are not linked to loss of REM atonia. Management includes bedroom safety, melatonin or low-dose clonazepam, and a review of antidepressants that can unmask the disorder.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a left ptotic eyelid and a small left pupil that dilates poorly in the dark, with ipsilateral facial anhidrosis after a neck injury. Which cocaine and apraclonidine testing pattern confirms the diagnosis?
options: Dilation with cocaine and failure with apraclonidine
Failure of dilation with both drops
Failure of dilation with cocaine and dilation with apraclonidine
items.explanation: Horner syndrome shows ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis from interruption of the sympathetic chain. Cocaine blocks norepinephrine reuptake, so it fails to dilate the affected pupil. Apraclonidine, a weak alpha-1 agonist, dilates through denervation supersensitivity. Neck trauma suggests carotid dissection, so urgent vascular imaging is also needed. Because the lesion may lie anywhere along a three neuron pathway, imaging of the head, neck, and chest is guided by associated findings.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a first migraine with unilateral weakness and aphasia lasting 40 minutes, followed by headache. A similar episode occurred in her mother. MRI and angiography are normal. What is the most appropriate caution?
options: Avoid estrogen-containing contraception and vasoconstricting abortives
Begin high-dose steroids for each attack
items.explanation: Hemiplegic migraine involves reversible motor weakness with aura, and familial forms are linked to CACNA1A, ATP1A2, and SCN1A mutations. Estrogen contraception and, traditionally, triptans are avoided because of stroke concern. Anticoagulation has no role once stroke and dissection are excluded, and steroids are unnecessary. Genetic testing is rarely necessary for diagnosis, and preventive options include verapamil, lamotrigine, acetazolamide, or antibodies, chosen individually.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman has excessive daytime sleepiness. Polysomnography shows normal sleep, and a multiple sleep latency test shows a mean latency of 6 minutes with no sleep-onset REM periods. She sleeps 11 hours nightly and wakes unrefreshed with sleep inertia. Which diagnosis fits?
items.explanation: Long, unrefreshing sleep with severe sleep inertia, short sleep latency, and fewer than two sleep-onset REM periods defines idiopathic hypersomnia. Narcolepsy type 1 has cataplexy or low hypocretin with REM onsets. Apnea would show events on polysomnography, and shift work disorder requires a rotating schedule. Treatment is largely symptomatic with wake-promoting drugs, and careful sleep scheduling and avoiding sedatives support daytime function.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with episodic migraine has two attacks a month, each treated successfully with sumatriptan. He now has coronary artery disease after a myocardial infarction. Which acute therapy is the most appropriate to offer instead?
options: A second triptan with a different half-life and a slower onset of action
Ergotamine tartrate combined with caffeine for each attack
A calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonist (gepant)
Rizatriptan with a lower starting dose
items.explanation: Triptans and ergots are vasoconstrictive and contraindicated in coronary disease, stroke, and uncontrolled hypertension. Gepants such as ubrogepant or rimegepant block the CGRP receptor without meaningful vasoconstriction, so they are suitable. Changing the triptan or its route does not remove the vascular risk, and ergotamine carries even greater vasoconstrictive liability. Always check cardiovascular risk before choosing between acute migraine drug classes, because that single factor usually decides the safest option.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man has a sudden severe headache three days after starting a decongestant and an antidepressant. Angiography shows segmental narrowing of cerebral arteries that resolves at 12 weeks. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
items.explanation: Recurrent thunderclap headaches with multifocal segmental vasoconstriction that reverses by 3 months define reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, triggered by serotonergic drugs, sympathomimetics, or the postpartum state. Angiitis follows a progressive course with abnormal cerebrospinal fluid, and moyamoya shows persistent stenosis. Repeat imaging after twelve weeks confirms reversal, and calcium channel blockers are sometimes used, while avoiding offending drugs is essential.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease and daily itching has an urge to move his legs at night. Ferritin is normal. Which finding best supports his symptoms as restless legs syndrome?
options: Symptoms occur only after prolonged standing
Symptoms start at rest, improve with movement, and are worse in the evening
items.explanation: The four essential criteria are an urge to move the legs, onset or worsening at rest, relief by movement, and an evening or night predominance. Uremia is a recognized secondary cause. Symptoms after standing, dermatomal pain, or relief when still would suggest venous disease, radiculopathy, or another cause. Dopamine and iron pathways are both implicated, and dialysis patients frequently benefit from managing anemia and avoiding aggravating drugs such as antihistamines.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic low back pain has taken oxycodone for 2 years at escalating doses with worsening function. Which step reflects sound opioid stewardship?
options: Taper gradually while adding nonopioid and nonpharmacologic therapy and consider naloxone access
Double the dose to improve function
Add a benzodiazepine for muscle spasm
items.explanation: When benefit does not outweigh harm, opioids are tapered slowly, with support, nonopioid analgesics, physical therapy, and attention to mood, while offering naloxone when risk is high. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal and pain flare, and dose escalation is not supported. Benzodiazepines combined with opioids increase respiratory depression and death. Documentation of function, urine drug testing when appropriate, and a clear shared plan keep care safe and protect the therapeutic relationship.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man treated with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor has increased dream enactment. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia. Which medication is the most appropriate treatment in addition to safety measures?
items.explanation: Melatonin, titrated up to 6 to 12 mg, is effective for REM sleep behavior disorder with a favorable side-effect profile in older adults. Clonazepam is an alternative but risks sedation, falls, and worsening apnea. Antihistamines and sedative hypnotics add confusion and fall risk without restoring REM atonia. Dose should be taken one to two hours before bedtime, and clonazepam can be considered if events persist, with monitoring in older patients.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man reports sudden sleep attacks while driving after starting a new drug for Parkinson disease. Which drug class is the likely cause?
options: Non-ergot dopamine agonist such as pramipexole
Monoamine oxidase B inhibitor such as rasagiline
items.explanation: Dopamine agonists, particularly pramipexole and ropinirole, are linked to sudden-onset sleep and excessive sleepiness. Counseling about driving and dose reduction are essential. Anticholinergics cause confusion, amantadine causes livedo and hallucinations, and MAO-B inhibitors seldom cause sleep attacks. Patients should be warned about driving, and sleepiness often improves when the agonist dose is lowered or an alternative drug is used.

items.stem: A 16-year-old boy has cataplexy and daytime sleepiness. Which drug treats cataplexy by inhibiting norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake?
items.explanation: Serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors such as venlafaxine suppress REM phenomena and reduce cataplexy, as do sodium oxybate and pitolisant. Modafinil and methylphenidate treat sleepiness without direct effect on cataplexy, and zolpidem is a hypnotic. Abrupt withdrawal of an antidepressant used for cataplexy risks rebound cataplexy, so doses are tapered gradually when stopping, and cataplexy diaries help track response.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with syncope has orthostatic hypotension on active standing. Which medication on his list is most likely contributing?
items.explanation: Alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin reduce vascular tone and commonly cause orthostatic hypotension, as do diuretics, vasodilators, and tricyclics. Levothyroxine in proper dosing, metformin, and acetaminophen do not typically lower standing blood pressure. Medication review is an essential early step. Stopping or switching the offending drug, rising slowly, and adequate hydration usually correct the problem without further testing in this setting.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman with migraine has attacks that last 3 days despite triptan use, and each recurs the next day after initial relief. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Add a long-acting nonsteroidal drug or a second dose of triptan with early dosing
items.explanation: Headache recurrence is common with short-acting triptans, and options include earlier dosing, a longer-acting triptan such as frovatriptan or naratriptan, or combining a triptan with a nonsteroidal drug. Barbiturate and opioid products promote overuse headache and are not advised as routine therapy. Long-acting preparations and early treatment while the pain is mild reduce recurrence, and limiting acute drug days prevents overuse headache.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman develops urinary retention, constipation, and dilated pupils poorly reactive to light and accommodation, after a viral illness. Antibodies to the ganglionic acetylcholine receptor are positive. What is the diagnosis?
options: Pure autonomic failure with low norepinephrine
items.explanation: Subacute pandysautonomia with antibodies against the alpha-3 ganglionic acetylcholine receptor defines autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy, treated with immunotherapy such as intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange. Botulism is a descending paralysis, and Lambert-Eaton involves proximal weakness with calcium channel antibodies. Antibody titers correlate with severity, and prompt immunotherapy often improves outcome, so identifying the condition early is clinically valuable.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a 3-year history of chronic insomnia has failed cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia and wants a medication. Which agent is acceptable with fewer cognitive adverse effects in older adults?
options: Diazepam at bedtime, nightly, at a standard adult dose
A dual orexin receptor antagonist such as suvorexant
items.explanation: Dual orexin receptor antagonists block wake-promoting signaling and carry lower risk of falls and dependence than benzodiazepines. Their adverse effects include somnolence and, rarely, complex sleep behaviors. Long-acting benzodiazepines accumulate, antihistamines are anticholinergic and potentially inappropriate in older adults, and tricyclics add cardiac and cognitive risk. Caution is required with sleep walking history and depression, and the lowest effective dose should be reviewed periodically and tapered when possible.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has phantom limb pain 3 months after an amputation below the knee. Which approach is best supported for management?
options: Neuropathic pain drugs plus mirror therapy or graded motor imagery
Observation, since it always resolves in weeks
Resection of the stump neuroma without trial of therapy
items.explanation: Phantom limb pain is a neuropathic pain treated with gabapentinoids or tricyclics, and behavioral approaches such as mirror therapy help. Opioids offer limited long-term benefit and carry risk. It does not always resolve spontaneously, and surgery is considered only when a specific, symptomatic neuroma remains after conservative treatment. Pain from the residual limb is distinct from phantom sensations, so examination of the stump and prosthetic fit is part of the evaluation.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic insomnia for 8 months has no sleep apnea or mood disorder. Which treatment is recommended first?
options: Nightly benzodiazepine at the lowest dose
items.explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, including stimulus control and sleep restriction, is first-line therapy for chronic insomnia with durable benefit. Medications are second line and short term. Benzodiazepines risk tolerance, falls, and dependence, antihistamines lose effect quickly and cause confusion in older adults, and trazodone has limited evidence at those doses. Techniques include fixed wake time, limiting time in bed, and removing stimulating activities, and benefits persist after treatment ends, unlike medication.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has chronic tension-type headache on more than 15 days a month. Which preventive drug has the best supporting evidence?
items.explanation: Amitriptyline is the best-studied preventive for chronic tension-type headache, with mirtazapine and venlafaxine as alternatives. Triptans do not help tension-type headache, carbamazepine is for neuralgias, and indomethacin is reserved for its responsive syndromes. Nonpharmacologic measures such as biofeedback and exercise add benefit. Nonpharmacologic measures such as relaxation training, biofeedback, and regular exercise add benefit, and medication should be started low and increased slowly.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman develops burning pain, hyperalgesia, and sweating changes in the left arm weeks after a left thalamic hemorrhage. Which drug class is most appropriate for central poststroke pain?
items.explanation: Central poststroke pain results from damage along the spinothalamic and thalamocortical pathways, and first-line options include amitriptyline and lamotrigine, with gabapentinoids as alternatives. Anti-inflammatory drugs act on nociceptive pain, steroids are not effective, and triptans are for migraine. Imaging of the brain is needed to confirm the lesion, and dose escalation should be gradual because sedation and dizziness are common in the early weeks.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with unilateral continuous headache, ptosis, and miosis has no response to oxygen. Which feature most strongly suggests a carotid dissection?
options: Ipsilateral neck pain with Horner syndrome after minor trauma
items.explanation: Painful Horner syndrome from disruption of the sympathetic fibers along the carotid artery is the classic presentation of carotid dissection, with ischemic stroke risk, and requires urgent vascular imaging. Migraine and stabbing headaches do not show this pattern, and chewing pain suggests jaw claudication or temporomandibular disease. Early antithrombotic therapy is started once hemorrhage and aneurysm are excluded, and the dissection is followed with repeat imaging.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant has a new severe headache with blood pressure 162/108 mm Hg, visual scotomata, and proteinuria. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat as preeclampsia with severe features: magnesium sulfate and blood pressure control
items.explanation: Headache with hypertension and proteinuria late in pregnancy indicates preeclampsia, which risks eclampsia and posterior reversible encephalopathy. Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures, and urgent antihypertensive therapy and obstetric planning follow. Ergotamine and triptans worsen vasoconstriction and are unsafe here. Delivery is the definitive treatment, so timing is planned with obstetric colleagues, and postpartum monitoring continues because eclampsia can occur after birth.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has episodic sweating, pallor, and a drop in standing blood pressure 30 minutes after meals. What mechanism explains this?
options: Postprandial splanchnic pooling with inadequate sympathetic compensation
Primary adrenal hyperfunction with catecholamine excess
Increased vagal tone causing bradycardia and syncope
Cerebral vasospasm after eating a meal
items.explanation: After eating, blood pools in the splanchnic bed, and failure of sympathetic vasoconstriction produces hypotension in autonomic failure. Smaller meals, fluids before eating, and caffeine can help. The other options do not explain meal-related drops in standing pressure. Treatment includes smaller meals with lower carbohydrate content, taking water before eating, and avoiding hot environments after meals.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has recurrent unilateral pulsating headaches lasting 8 to 24 hours with nausea and photophobia. Twenty minutes before each attack she sees a shimmering zigzag in the left visual field that spreads and resolves over 25 minutes. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Occipital lobe epilepsy with postictal headache
items.explanation: Fully reversible visual symptoms that develop gradually over at least 5 minutes and last under 60 minutes, followed by headache, define migraine with typical aura. Occipital seizures produce brief, colored, circular phenomena lasting seconds to a couple of minutes. Cluster headache is short and agitating without march-type aura. Retinal migraine is monocular and fully reversible in one eye, whereas this field disturbance is homonymous.

items.stem: Which test best measures sympathetic postganglionic sudomotor function in a patient with suspected small fiber autonomic neuropathy?
options: Heart rate response to deep breathing
Valsalva ratio with beat to beat pressure
Tilt table test with continuous monitoring
items.explanation: The quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test measures postganglionic sweat output after acetylcholine iontophoresis and assesses small fiber integrity. Deep breathing and Valsalva ratio assess cardiovagal function, and tilt testing examines cardiovascular adrenergic responses, so they do not test sweating. Results are combined with other autonomic tests, and skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density gives structural confirmation of small fiber neuropathy.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with trigeminal neuralgia is found to have loss of facial sensation over the left cheek and an abnormal corneal reflex. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance since examination findings are expected in classical neuralgia
MRI of the brain with attention to the trigeminal nerve and brainstem
items.explanation: Sensory loss in a trigeminal neuralgia pattern indicates secondary neuralgia, from causes such as multiple sclerosis plaque, tumor in the cerebellopontine angle, or arteriovenous malformation. Imaging is required. Reassurance or dose escalation misses a structural lesion, and destructive procedures should wait until the cause is clarified. MRI with thin sections through the brainstem and cerebellopontine angle can show demyelination, tumor, or vascular compression that changes treatment and surgical planning.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought for sleepwalking. Her episodes begin about 90 minutes after sleep onset, last 10 minutes, and she cannot recall them. Which sleep stage do these events arise from?
items.explanation: Disorders of arousal such as sleepwalking and sleep terrors arise from N3 sleep, concentrated in the first third of the night when slow wave sleep is most abundant, with amnesia for the event. REM parasomnias occur later with dream enactment. Stage N1 is a brief transitional stage, and confusional arousals do not arise from full wakefulness.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has dull headache every morning that is worse with coughing and bending, with vomiting and progressive memory complaints over 6 weeks. What is the next best step?
items.explanation: A progressive positional headache with vomiting and cognitive change signals raised intracranial pressure from a mass lesion until proven otherwise, so contrast neuroimaging is essential. Triptans treat primary migraine, and plain neck films or EEG would not detect an intracranial mass. Papilledema on funduscopy would add urgency, and neurosurgical referral follows if a mass is found, with steroids used for edema.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes has early satiety, vomiting of undigested food, and unpredictable glucose. Which autonomic problem is most likely?
options: Pyloric stenosis from peptic ulcer scarring
Diabetic gastroparesis from vagal autonomic neuropathy
Cyclic vomiting syndrome with a migraine link
items.explanation: Long-standing diabetes damages vagal parasympathetic fibers, delaying gastric emptying. Gastric emptying scintigraphy confirms the diagnosis, and management involves small meals, glycemic control, and prokinetics such as metoclopramide, with caution for tardive dyskinesia. Mechanical obstruction and ischemia need imaging, and cyclic vomiting occurs in discrete stereotyped bouts. Glycemic variability worsens emptying, so tight glucose management, avoiding opioids and anticholinergics, and dietary texture changes are part of the plan.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has an urge to move her legs in the evening, relieved by walking, with worsening at rest. Ferritin is 28 ng/mL. Which is the best initial approach?
options: Start a nighttime opioid at once
Oral or intravenous iron repletion, since ferritin should be above 75 ng/mL
items.explanation: Restless legs syndrome is linked to brain iron deficiency, and guidelines advise iron when ferritin is 75 ng/mL or below. Alpha-2-delta ligands such as gabapentin enacarbil or pregabalin are preferred drugs, and dopamine agonists risk augmentation, so high-dose use is discouraged. Hypnotics do not treat the urge, and opioids are reserved for refractory disease. Iron indices should be rechecked every few months, and use of antihistamines, antidepressants, or dopamine antagonists that worsen symptoms should be reviewed.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and supine hypertension needs treatment for symptomatic standing hypotension. Which drug is approved for this indication?
items.explanation: Midodrine, an alpha-1 agonist, and droxidopa, a norepinephrine prodrug, are approved for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and fludrocortisone is used off label. Both worsen supine hypertension, so the patient should avoid lying flat and take doses during the day. Propranolol, clonidine, and diuretics lower pressure or volume and would worsen the problem. Supine blood pressure should be checked at bedtime and head-of-bed elevation used, because the drug raises pressure while lying flat.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has excessive sweating of his palms and axillae since adolescence that interferes with work. There is no weight loss or night sweating. What is the first-line treatment?
options: Surgical sympathectomy of the thoracic chain
items.explanation: Primary focal hyperhidrosis is treated first with topical aluminum chloride antiperspirants. Iontophoresis, botulinum toxin injections, and oral anticholinergics follow, and sympathectomy is reserved for refractory palmar disease because of compensatory sweating. Steroids and beta-blockers do not address the cholinergic sweat gland overactivity. Treatment choice should be reviewed when sweating is generalized or nocturnal, because lymphoma, thyroid disease, and infection need exclusion in that setting.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with episodic cluster headache is considered for prophylaxis. He has been in a bout for 10 days. Which short-term bridging therapy is appropriate?
options: A short course of oral prednisone or a greater occipital nerve block
items.explanation: Because verapamil takes weeks to act, short courses of corticosteroids or occipital nerve blocks provide rapid suppression during the transition. Chronic ergotamine and opioids are unsuitable for long-term use, and aspirin does not abort or prevent cluster headache. Preventive therapy takes weeks to act, so the bridging treatment is stopped once the preventive reaches effect or the bout ends.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has sudden, worst-ever headache reaching maximal intensity within a minute, while lifting weights. Noncontrast head CT performed 3 hours after onset is normal. What is the next best step?
options: Lumbar puncture, or CT angiography if puncture is declined
Discharge on analgesics with follow-up in a week
Repeat CT in 24 hours without further testing or vascular imaging at any point
items.explanation: Thunderclap headache requires exclusion of subarachnoid hemorrhage and other vascular causes. Modern CT within 6 hours is highly sensitive but must meet strict conditions; otherwise a lumbar puncture seeking xanthochromia or red cells, or vascular imaging, is needed. Discharge risks a missed aneurysm, and a triptan could worsen reversible vasoconstriction syndrome. Time since onset matters, so the interval between symptom start and scanning should be documented before deciding that a normal scan is sufficient.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction, and rapidly progressive parkinsonism with cerebellar ataxia and stridor. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Early severe autonomic failure with parkinsonism, cerebellar signs, and laryngeal stridor defines multiple system atrophy, a synucleinopathy with oligodendroglial inclusions. Pure autonomic failure lacks motor findings. Diabetic neuropathy needs diabetes, and typical Parkinson disease responds well to levodopa and has late, milder autonomic problems. Autonomic testing and MRI showing a hot cross bun sign in the pons or putaminal changes support the diagnosis, which carries a faster course than Parkinson disease.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman faints after standing in a hot crowded room, preceded by nausea, sweating, and tunnel vision, with rapid recovery on lying down. Cardiac examination and ECG are normal. What is the best counseling?
options: Implant a permanent pacemaker and arrange electrophysiology follow-up now
Reassurance, hydration, and counterpressure maneuvers at the onset of symptoms
items.explanation: Typical vasovagal syncope has clear triggers and prodrome, quick recovery, and normal heart evaluation. Education, fluids, salt, and counterpressure maneuvers such as leg crossing or hand grip prevent recurrence. Pacemakers, anticoagulants, and antiepileptics are not indicated for uncomplicated reflex syncope. Recurrent unexplained episodes, exertional faint, or abnormal ECG would prompt cardiac evaluation, but none of these appear in this picture.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman develops headache within 15 minutes of sitting up that resolves when she lies flat. Two weeks earlier she had chiropractic neck manipulation. MRI shows diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and brain sag. What is the most likely cause?
options: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension with papilledema and raised opening pressure
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a cerebrospinal fluid leak
Chronic subdural hygroma from trauma only
Cervical artery dissection with hemispheric stroke
items.explanation: Orthostatic headache with diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and downward brain displacement is characteristic of cerebrospinal fluid volume loss. Spinal imaging finds the leak, and treatment begins with rest, hydration, and caffeine, then an epidural blood patch. Intracranial hypertension worsens when lying, and dissection would present with neck pain and focal deficits. Imaging of the spine, often with myelography, finds the leak, and persistent cases may require targeted patching or surgical repair by specialists.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with Parkinson disease has marked daytime sleepiness. Polysomnography shows periodic limb movements and REM sleep without atonia. What contributes most to her sleepiness?
options: Dopamine agonist therapy and fragmented nocturnal sleep
Hypothyroidism with myxedema as the sole cause
items.explanation: Sleepiness in Parkinson disease arises from the disease itself and from dopamine agonists, which can cause sleep attacks, along with sleep fragmentation from limb movements and REM behavior disorder. Narcolepsy with cataplexy and primary insomnia do not explain this picture. Reducing the dopamine agonist, treating periodic limb movements, and improving nocturnal sleep may lessen sleepiness, and stimulants can be added when needed.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a multiple sleep latency test showing a mean sleep latency of 5 minutes and three sleep-onset REM periods, after a night of polysomnography with 7 hours of sleep and no apnea. She has no cataplexy. Which diagnosis is most appropriate?
items.explanation: A mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep-onset REM periods, with a sleep-onset REM on the preceding polysomnogram counting toward the total, supports narcolepsy. Without cataplexy or low hypocretin, this is type 2. Idiopathic hypersomnia shows long sleep and few REM onsets. Insufficient sleep and circadian delay must be excluded by diary and actigraphy.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has burning, shooting pain and allodynia in both feet from diabetic polyneuropathy. She has no cardiac disease and takes no other medications. Which is an appropriate first-line drug?
items.explanation: Gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors such as duloxetine and venlafaxine are first-line therapy for painful diabetic neuropathy. Opioids and tramadol are reserved because of misuse and limited long-term benefit. Acetaminophen and steroids have no meaningful effect on neuropathic pain. Starting dose should be low and titrated, and blood pressure and nausea monitored, as tolerance often develops over the first weeks.

items.stem: A 21-year-old man cannot fall asleep before 3 a.m. and cannot wake before 11 a.m. on weekdays or weekends. When allowed to keep this schedule he sleeps normally. Which treatment best shifts his rhythm?
options: Evening bright light with a morning dose of melatonin taken on waking
Evening low-dose melatonin with bright light on waking
Nightly zolpidem at the desired bedtime
items.explanation: Delayed sleep phase disorder is treated by advancing the rhythm: melatonin about 5 hours before habitual sleep onset or a few hours before desired bedtime, plus bright light shortly after waking. Reversing the timing would push the rhythm later. Naps and stimulants do not correct phase, and hypnotics treat symptoms without realigning circadian timing. Timing matters more than dose, so give the melatonin hours before sleep and keep wake time fixed, including on weekends, for lasting realignment.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with Parkinson disease has urinary urgency and incontinence. Postvoid residual volume is 30 mL. Which medication class needs the most caution?
options: Anticholinergic bladder agents, because of cognitive risk
items.explanation: Detrusor overactivity is common in Parkinson disease, but anticholinergic bladder drugs cross the blood-brain barrier and can precipitate confusion and hallucinations. Beta-3 agonists, behavioral therapy, and pelvic exercises avoid that risk. A low residual rules out retention, which would change the plan. Catheterization may be needed if residual volume rises, and orthostatic hypotension and constipation should be managed alongside the bladder symptoms.
